description: TAI Julian Dates converted to UT1, cross-checked against astropy. UT1 is the one scale here resting on published data rather than on a definition, and astropy and the iers gem read different tables, so astropy is no oracle for the value: at J2000 the two tables' delta UT1 are about 17 microseconds apart. It is still an oracle for the arithmetic. Each case carries the delta T the conversion is to use, and the test injects it through Configuration#eop_source so both sides start from one number. astropy reaches UT1 as UTC + delta UT1, Horologium as TT - delta T, and the two agree to well under a nanosecond. The cases sit in the measured era, from 1973 on, where a published delta UT1 exists to feed both sides; the polynomial era before it is covered by the unit tests instead.

source.method: astropy.time.Time(jd1, jd2, format='jd', scale='tai') with delta_ut1_utc set to IERS::UT1.at(mjd:).ut1_utc read at the UTC date Horologium indexes delta T by, UT1 read as .ut1.jd1/.ut1.jd2. Each delta_t is (TAI - UTC) + 32.184 - delta UT1 at that same date, the same input written the way Horologium consumes it.
